programs.name: Stay NJ
programs.tagline: Up to $6,500 back on property taxes for New Jersey homeowners 65 and older
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ and owns their New Jersey home, Stay NJ can pay back part of their property taxes. The most it pays is $6,500 a year with income of $100,000 or less, $5,000 with income up to $150,000, and $4,000 with income up to $200,000. Over $200,000 the benefit is $0.

Stay NJ is for older homeowners with income of $200,000 or less who lived in their home for the full previous year. Because one application (PAS-1) covers multiple New Jersey tax relief programs, the state automatically determines which benefits your loved one qualifies for, they may receive Stay NJ plus additional programs like ANCHOR or Senior Freeze for even more savings.
programs.savingsRange: Up to $6,500 a year (income $100,000 or less); up to $5,000 ($100,000-$150,000); up to $4,000 ($150,000-$200,000). The 2025 benefit is paid in February and May 2027.
programs.savingsSource: Maximum benefit by income tier ($6,500 / $5,000 / $4,000), paid quarterly; total relief cannot exceed property taxes paid.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for Stay NJ if they moved to their current home in the middle of last year?
faqs.answer: No. Your loved one must have owned and lived in the home as their principal residence for the full 12 months of the prior year. If they moved in July, they'd need to wait until the following application cycle to meet the full-year requirement.

faqs.question: What if my loved one owns a mobile home and pays property taxes on it?
faqs.answer: Mobile homeowners are specifically excluded from Stay NJ, even if they pay property taxes or are assessed like traditional homeowners. This exclusion is explicit in the program rules.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one who has difficulty with online applications?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can help your loved one apply, but the application must be in their name and use their information. You can print the PAS-1 form and mail it to the New Jersey Division of Taxation if online access is difficult, though only online filers can get direct deposit, and only for some payments.

faqs.question: How much will my loved one actually receive?
faqs.answer: It depends on income and on the property taxes paid. The most Stay NJ pays is $6,500 with income of $100,000 or less, $5,000 with income up to $150,000, and $4,000 with income up to $200,000. Total property tax relief from all programs cannot be more than the property taxes paid on the home.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get Stay NJ and ANCHOR benefits at the same time?
faqs.answer: The state determines which combination of benefits your loved one receives based on their PAS-1 application. Many people qualify for multiple programs simultaneously, Stay NJ, ANCHOR, and Senior Freeze can often be combined for maximum tax relief.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income is close to the $200,000 limit?
faqs.answer: The income limit is based on the prior year's state tax return, so use that year's actual income. If your loved one's income fluctuates around the limit, apply anyway, the state will make the determination based on the specific tax year's income.

programs.name: Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement)
programs.tagline: Get reimbursed for property tax increases if your loved one is 65+ and has lived in their New Jersey home for years

localEntities.name: NJ Division of Taxation (statewide)

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ and has lived in their New Jersey home since at least 2016, they may get reimbursed for property tax increases above what they paid in their first qualifying year. Income limit: $99,735 or less for 2025 applications (combined for married couples).

This isn't a tax freeze, it's a reimbursement program. Your loved one still pays the full property tax bill, but the state reimburses them for increases above their "base year" amount. Because New Jersey administers this through one combined application (PAS-1), your loved one can apply for Senior Freeze, ANCHOR, and Stay NJ benefits all at once.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for Senior Freeze and ANCHOR at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, the PAS-1 application covers Senior Freeze, ANCHOR, and Stay NJ all in one form. The state will determine which programs your loved one qualifies for and send a letter explaining their benefits.

faqs.question: What if my loved one moved within New Jersey since 2016?
faqs.answer: They may still qualify if they received Senior Freeze reimbursement for their prior New Jersey residence in the last full year they lived there. Contact (800) 882-6597 to discuss their specific situation.

faqs.question: Does the income limit include both spouses?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your loved ones are married or in a civil union and living together, their combined income cannot exceed $99,735 for 2025 applications. The limit applies to their total household income.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one missed the eligibility requirements for one year?
faqs.answer: They must meet all requirements every year from their base year through the application year. If they missed even one year, they may lose eligibility and would need to restart with a new base year if they qualify again.

programs.name: Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC)
programs.tagline: Helps parents age 60+ who need nursing-level care stay at home when they don't qualify for Medicaid.

localEntities.name: County Aging and Disability Resource Connections via 1-877-222-3737
Examples: Hunterdon Human Services (908-788-1361), Warren Division of Aging (908-475-6591), FCS Monmouth/Mercer/Ocean[2][3][7]

programs.intro:
If your loved one needs daily help with bathing, dressing, or medication management but earns too much for Medicaid, JACC provides up to $1,156 monthly in home care services. This New Jersey program serves people 60+ who need nursing facility level care but want to stay in their own homes.

JACC covers personal care, homemaking, and care management through a personalized Plan of Care. Because the program includes Participant-Employed Provider (PEP) options, your loved one can hire family members or friends as their caregivers. You'll pay a sliding-scale co-pay based on income, but the program covers the majority of costs.

The catch: JACC is specifically for people who don't qualify for Medicaid waiver services like MLTSS. Income limit is 365% of Federal Poverty Level (around $3,300/month for individuals), and assets must be under $40,000 for individuals or $60,000 for couples.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for JACC if they currently receive some Medicaid benefits?
faqs.answer: No, JACC is specifically for people who are financially ineligible for Medicaid or Medicaid waiver services like MLTSS. If your loved one qualifies for any Medicaid long-term care services, they cannot receive JACC. However, they may be able to receive JACC for services not covered by their current Medicaid benefits - ask during the assessment.

faqs.question: Can I hire myself as my loved one's caregiver through the Participant-Employed Provider option?
faqs.answer: Yes, the PEP option allows your loved one to hire family members or friends as their paid caregivers. You'll need to complete provider training and meet program requirements. This option gives families more control over who provides care and when.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income or assets change after they're approved?
faqs.answer: You must report changes in income or assets to your care manager. Significant increases might affect eligibility or co-pay amounts. Your Plan of Care is reviewed periodically, and changes in financial status could impact services.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really, and are there priority categories?
faqs.answer: Waitlist times vary significantly by county and current funding levels. Some areas have immediate openings while others may have several month waits. The program operates on available funding, so ask your county office about current wait times and whether any priority categories apply.

faqs.question: What's the difference between JACC and regular Medicaid home care?
faqs.answer: JACC serves people who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid but still need nursing-level care at home. Unlike Medicaid, JACC has higher income limits (365% FPL vs. Medicaid's much lower limits) and asset limits ($40,000 individual vs. Medicaid's $2,000), but requires co-pays and has monthly service caps.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than the asset limits?
faqs.answer: The home you live in is typically not counted toward the $40,000/$60,000 asset limits for JACC eligibility. However, the specific rules about what assets are exempt aren't detailed in available sources, so ask your care manager during the application process about how your loved one's home equity affects eligibility.

faqs.question: What specific services does the monthly cap cover, and what doesn't it include?
faqs.answer: The $1,090-$1,156 monthly cap covers services in your personalized Plan of Care, such as personal care assistance, homemaking, and care management. Medical care, prescription drugs, and equipment typically aren't covered - those remain your responsibility through Medicare or other insurance.

faqs.question: Can we apply while my loved one is still in the hospital or rehab facility?
faqs.answer: You can start the application process while your loved one is in a facility, but JACC services can only begin once they're living in qualifying community housing (their own home or unlicensed home of family/friend). Discharge planners may be able to help coordinate the transition and application timing.

programs.name: Pharmaceutical Assistance to the Aged & Disabled (PAAD)
programs.tagline: If your loved one lives in New Jersey and earns less than $54,943/year, they may qualify for $5-7 prescription copays instead of full drug prices.

localEntities.name: Central processing in Trenton; pharmacies statewide accept PAAD

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ or disabled and lives in New Jersey, PAAD can dramatically reduce their prescription costs. Instead of paying full price for medications, they'll pay just $5 per generic drug and $7 per brand-name drug, PAAD covers the rest. This applies to all FDA-approved prescription medications, insulin, and insulin supplies.

Income limit for 2026: $54,943 or less if single, $62,390 or less if married. Because there are no asset limits, your loved one can qualify even if they own their home or have savings. The catch: if they're Medicare-eligible, they must enroll in a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, and PAAD will pay the premium for qualifying low-cost plans.

Because PAAD works alongside Medicare Part D rather than replacing it, your loved one gets the broad coverage of Medicare's formulary with the low copays of a state assistance program. One team at the state level manages both the prescription benefits and Part D premium payments.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for both PAAD and Senior Gold?
faqs.answer: No, your loved one can only be enrolled in one program at a time. PAAD has lower income limits ($54,943 single/$62,390 married) with $5 generic/$7 brand copays. Senior Gold has higher income limits but different copay structures. Apply for PAAD first if income-eligible since the copays are lower.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's Medicare Part D plan has a high premium?
faqs.answer: PAAD only pays premiums for plans at or near the regional benchmark (typically the lowest-cost plans in your area). If your loved one chooses a more expensive plan, they may lose premium assistance but can still get the $5/$7 copays. Call 1-800-792-9745 to find qualifying low-premium plans before enrolling.

faqs.question: Does PAAD cover diabetic test strips and supplies?
faqs.answer: No, PAAD does not cover diabetic testing supplies or most supplies covered by Medicare Part B. It covers FDA-approved prescription drugs, insulin, insulin supplies, and syringes/needles for multiple sclerosis injectables only. Your loved one would need to rely on Medicare Part B or other insurance for test strips.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can help complete the application, especially if your loved one has difficulty with paperwork or technology. You can apply online at NJSaves.org or complete the AP-2 form by mail. You'll need access to all their financial and medical documentation.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's medication isn't covered by their Medicare Part D plan?
faqs.answer: PAAD cannot override Medicare Part D formulary restrictions. If a medication isn't covered, you must first request an exception or prior authorization through the Medicare Part D plan. If approved by Part D, then PAAD will provide the $5/$7 copay. Call your Part D plan directly for exception requests.

faqs.question: Will owning a house or having savings disqualify my loved one?
faqs.answer: No, PAAD has no asset limits. Your loved one can own their home, have bank accounts, investments, or other assets and still qualify. Only income matters for eligibility, $54,943 or less for singles, $62,390 or less for married couples in 2026.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one moves from New Jersey to another state?
faqs.answer: PAAD benefits end when your loved one is no longer a New Jersey resident. They would need to apply for prescription assistance programs in their new state. Make sure to notify PAAD of the address change and ask about the effective date of termination.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get PAAD if they have Medicaid or are applying for it?
faqs.answer: No, PAAD eligibility specifically excludes people who have Medicaid. If your loved one is considering both programs, compare the prescription benefits, Medicaid typically has very low copays already. If they lose Medicaid eligibility later, they can then apply for PAAD.

programs.name: Lifeline Credit
programs.tagline: Up to $225/year off your loved one's electric and gas bills if they're 65+ and qualify for prescription assistance.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+ and already gets New Jersey's prescription assistance (PAAD) or receives SSI, they qualify for up to $225/year off their electric and natural gas bills. The Lifeline Credit appears automatically on their utility bill, no monthly paperwork or vouchers to manage.

For 2026, your loved one qualifies if their annual gross income is below $54,943 (single) or $62,390 (married). They must be a residential electric or gas customer, the program doesn't cover oil, propane, or other heating sources. Only one person per household can receive the credit.

SSI recipients get this benefit automatically in their monthly check and don't need to apply separately. Everyone else applies through the same NJSave application used for prescription assistance, making it a simple add-on to programs your loved one may already use.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get Lifeline Credit if they heat with oil or propane?
faqs.answer: No. Lifeline Credit only applies to residential electric and natural gas customers. Homes heated with oil, propane, wood, or coal don't qualify for this program. Look into LIHEAP energy assistance instead, which covers all heating sources.

faqs.question: What if both my loved ones live together, can they both apply?
faqs.answer: No. Only one person per household can receive Lifeline Credit, even if both parents meet the age and income requirements. The application must be in the name of the person who pays the utility bills or their spouse.

faqs.question: My loved one gets SSI, do they still need to apply for Lifeline Credit?
faqs.answer: No. SSI recipients get the Lifeline Credit automatically as part of their monthly SSI payment. They should not submit a separate application for this program.

faqs.question: Can I apply for both PAAD prescription assistance and Lifeline Credit at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. The NJSave application covers both programs. When you apply for PAAD, the Lifeline Credit questions are included in the same application, making it a simple one-stop process.

faqs.question: How does the credit appear on the utility bill?
faqs.answer: The annual credit of up to $225 appears directly on your loved one's electric and/or natural gas bill. There are no vouchers to redeem or separate payments to manage, the utility company applies the credit automatically.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income goes up after they're approved?
faqs.answer: Eligibility is typically checked annually as of July 1st. If your loved one's income rises above the limits ($54,943 for single, $62,390 for married), they'll need to report the change and may lose eligibility for the following year.

faqs.question: My loved one already gets the automatic application in the mail, do they still need to reapply each year?
faqs.answer: Yes. Even though MAA, MAO, and New Jersey Care beneficiaries receive applications automatically each August, they must complete and return the form annually to continue receiving the Lifeline Credit.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get Lifeline Credit if they're not a U.S. citizen?
faqs.answer: Yes. U.S. citizenship is not required for Lifeline Credit. Your loved one only needs to be a New Jersey resident who meets the age, income, and utility customer requirements.

programs.name: New Jersey Statewide Respite Care Program
programs.tagline: If you're caring for a disabled loved one in New Jersey, get paid companion care, overnight help, or adult day services to give you a break.
programs.intro:
If you're providing daily care for a loved one with a chronic disability or illness in New Jersey, you may qualify for companion care, overnight help, adult day services, or even short-term facility placement to give you respite. Because this program covers in-home care, nursing services, and temporary placement options, your loved one can get the supervision they need while you take a break or handle other responsibilities.

Your loved one must receive daily care from you (unpaid) and have functional impairments certified by their doctor. Income limit: $2,982/month for a single person, $5,964/month for married couples in 2026. Asset limit: $40,000 for single, $60,000 for couples. programs.intro:
If your aging parent is 65 or older (or is blind or disabled) and their income and savings are not enough to cover their medical care, NJ FamilyCare ABD may provide full Medicaid health coverage at little or no cost. The program is designed specifically for people whose resources fall short of what care actually costs.

NJ FamilyCare ABD is not a single plan; it is a set of Medicaid pathways, each with its own rules around income and assets. One pathway, the Medicaid Only Program, is for people who do not receive SSI but whose income and resources fall under SSI standards. Because eligibility depends on which pathway applies to your parent's situation, the most reliable way to know if they qualify is to submit an application.

Applications are handled by your parent's county social service agency. The state program is uniform across New Jersey, but county offices manage the paperwork, may request different supporting documents, and have their own processing timelines. Based on one county's published timeline, processing has been taking roughly 6 to 12 weeks, though this varies. Apply as soon as possible because coverage cannot begin before the application date.

contentSections.heading: This is not one program; it is a set of Medicaid pathways.
contentSections.body: NJ FamilyCare ABD covers several eligibility tracks, including one for people who receive SSI and others for people who do not but still have limited income and resources. Because the rules differ by track, the state's own guidance says the only way to know for sure if your parent qualifies is to apply. Do not assume your parent doesn't qualify based on income alone without checking.

contentSections.body: Official NJ FamilyCare materials confirm that income and countable resources are evaluated, and that the Medicaid Only pathway follows SSI standards, but a full statewide income and asset chart is not available in a single published document. Call 1-800-356-1561 or contact your county social service agency to get current figures before deciding whether to apply.

faqs.question: My parent's income is above SSI limits. Does that automatically disqualify them?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. NJ FamilyCare ABD includes multiple eligibility pathways, and not all of them use SSI income limits as a hard cutoff. Some pathways allow for deductions or spend-down arrangements that can reduce countable income on paper. The official guidance says the only way to know for certain is to apply. Call 1-800-356-1561 to get a screening before assuming your parent doesn't qualify.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my parent's behalf if they cannot manage the process themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or authorized representative can complete and submit the application. If you are acting as a legal representative (through power of attorney or guardianship), bring those legal documents along with the application materials. Contact your county social service agency at 1-800-356-1561 to confirm what documentation they require for a representative filing.

faqs.question: Will my parent's house count against them when determining asset eligibility?
faqs.answer: The primary home is generally treated as an exempt asset under Medicaid rules, meaning it typically does not count against eligibility while your parent lives there. However, exact rules around home equity, co-ownership, and what happens if your parent moves out are complex and vary by circumstance. Do not assume the home is automatically excluded in every situation. Ask the county social service agency to walk through your parent's specific case.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for NJ FamilyCare ABD and a Medicare Savings Program at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and doing both at once is often a smart move. Medicare Savings Programs help pay Medicare premiums for people with limited income, and they are administered through the same county social service agencies. When you contact your county office to apply for NJ FamilyCare ABD, ask whether your parent also qualifies for a Medicare Savings Program. One conversation can open both applications.

faqs.question: How long does it actually take to get a decision?
faqs.answer: At least one county has published a processing time of approximately 6 to 12 weeks, but this is not a statewide guarantee. Processing time depends on the county office's current workload and how quickly all required documents are submitted. Missing documents are the most common cause of delays. Ask your county office for their current timeline when you apply, and submit all documents at once to avoid back-and-forth.

faqs.question: My parent is a green card holder. Do they qualify?
faqs.answer: Qualified immigrants, including lawful permanent residents, may be eligible, but adult qualified immigrants generally must have held lawful permanent resident status for at least five years before applying. Some exceptions apply, including for people who are refugees or asylees. If your parent received their green card less than five years ago, call 1-800-356-1561 before assuming they are ineligible, because the immigration rules are specific and depend on the visa category.

programs.intro:
If your parent is 65 or older and needs daily help with bathing, dressing, medication management, or other personal care tasks, NJ FamilyCare MLTSS can cover the full cost of that care through New Jersey Medicaid. This is not just home care: it can include nursing facility care, assisted living, home modifications like wheelchair ramps, home-delivered meals, a personal emergency response system, and a dedicated care manager who coordinates every service under one plan.

The program works differently from a standard insurance plan. Once your parent qualifies, a NJ FamilyCare managed care organization takes over coordinating all covered medical and long-term care. Your parent gets one care team instead of separate doctors, agencies, and benefit offices. That coordination is included at no additional cost.

Qualifying requires passing two tests: a financial test (income and assets within Medicaid long-term-care limits) and a clinical test (a formal assessment showing your parent needs nursing-home-level care). Both tests must be met. Starting the process at your county Area Agency on Aging or Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) is the most reliable first step, because they conduct the clinical screening and can connect you directly to the financial eligibility process.

For adults 21+, eligibility screening starts through the county ADRC or Area Agency on Aging
Medicaid's five-year look-back period applies: asset transfers made within the past five years may create a period of ineligibility

applicationGuide.summary: Adults 21 and older should start by contacting their county Area Agency on Aging or ADRC, which conducts the required clinical screening before the financial application can be completed.

steps.title: Contact your county ADRC or Area Agency on Aging
steps.description: For adults 21 and older, call your county Area Agency on Aging or Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC). They conduct the required nursing-home level-of-care screening. You cannot complete the MLTSS process without this clinical assessment. Find your county ADRC at nj.gov/humanservices/doas/home or ask your county social services office for a referral.

steps.title: Complete the clinical level-of-care screening
steps.description: A screener will evaluate whether your parent needs nursing-home-level care based on their ability to perform daily activities such as bathing, dressing, eating, and medication management. This assessment happens before or alongside the financial application. Bring any medical records, physician statements, or current care plans that document your parent's needs.

steps.title: Submit the NJ FamilyCare financial application
steps.description: Apply online at njfamilycare.dhs.state.nj.us/apply.aspx, in person at your county social services or welfare agency, or by mail using the paper NJ FamilyCare application. Gather documents proving income, assets, residency, age, and citizenship before you apply. If your parent's income exceeds $2,982/month, ask the county office about establishing a Qualified Income Trust (QIT) before or at the same time as applying.

steps.title: Enroll with a NJ FamilyCare managed care organization (MCO)
steps.description: Once both eligibility determinations are approved, your parent will be enrolled in a NJ FamilyCare managed care plan. The MCO will assign a care manager who coordinates all covered services, including home care, nursing facility care if needed, meals, and medical services. You may have a choice of MCOs depending on your county.

steps.title: Work with the care manager to set up services
steps.description: After enrollment, the MCO care manager conducts an assessment of your parent's specific needs and develops an individual service plan. The services your parent receives, such as home modifications, personal care hours, respite care, or assisted living placement, depend on what that assessment finds, not just on the diagnosis or age.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Processing time is not a single fixed number. MLTSS requires completing both a clinical screening and a financial eligibility determination. Timing depends on how quickly both parts are completed and on your county and managed care plan. Ask your county ADRC and county social services office for current expected timelines when you begin.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No formal statewide waitlist is identified in the source material. Access depends on completing both the clinical screening and financial eligibility determination, then enrolling with a NJ FamilyCare managed care organization. Processing speed can vary by county.
applicationGuide.tip: Do not skip the county ADRC step and go straight to the online application. The financial application alone will not complete your parent's eligibility. The clinical screening must happen through the county ADRC or Area Agency on Aging, and missing it delays everything.

applicationNotes: If your parent is currently in a hospital or rehabilitation facility, the discharge planner or social worker can often initiate the MLTSS screening process before discharge. Ask specifically about MLTSS when planning discharge, because the program can sometimes prevent a permanent nursing home admission.

If your parent's income exceeds $2,982/month, do not assume they are ineligible. A Qualified Income Trust (QIT) allows excess income to be deposited monthly into a trust account and may restore eligibility. Setting up a QIT requires a legal document; ask the county social services office to explain the process and consider consulting an elder law attorney.

The $2,000 asset limit is measured on the first day of each month. If your parent has more than $2,000 in countable assets, they are ineligible for that month. Assets transferred within the past five years may be subject to Medicaid's look-back rules and could create a penalty period. This is one of the most consequential parts of the application; do not make financial transfers without understanding the look-back period first.

The services your parent actually receives after enrollment depend on the individual care assessment the managed care organization conducts, not just on the diagnosis or on having qualified for the program. More detailed documentation of your parent's daily care needs at the clinical screening stage can help ensure the full scope of needed services is captured in the care plan.

contentSections.title: Two tests, not one
contentSections.body: Many families apply for MLTSS through the financial application online and wait, not knowing the process is stalled because the clinical screening has not happened yet. Your parent must pass both a financial test (income and assets within Medicaid long-term-care limits) and a clinical test (a formal assessment that they need nursing-home-level care). Both must be completed. Start with your county ADRC or Area Agency on Aging to make sure the clinical screening is initiated first or in parallel.

contentSections.title: What services does MLTSS actually cover?
contentSections.body:
Once enrolled, your parent's managed care plan covers a broad range of services. These include personal care assistance at home, nursing facility care if needed, assisted living, care management (a single coordinator who manages all covered services), home and vehicle modifications such as ramps or grab bars, home-delivered meals, a personal emergency response system (a medical alert device), respite care for family caregivers, mental health and substance use services, and the full range of NJ FamilyCare Plan A health benefits including prescription drugs.

The specific services your parent receives depend on what the MCO's care assessment determines. A person with higher care needs will have a more intensive service plan than someone with lower needs. The care manager works with your family to identify what support is needed and helps arrange each service.

contentSections.title: Understanding the income rules
contentSections.body:
For 2026, Medicaid's monthly income limit for long-term-care eligibility is $2,982 for a single person. If your parent's income is at or below that amount, they may qualify based on income alone. If their income is above $2,982, they may still qualify by establishing a Qualified Income Trust (QIT, sometimes called a Miller Trust). Each month, the income above the limit is deposited into the QIT account rather than used freely, and Medicaid treats the person as if their income is within limits.

Setting up a QIT requires a legal trust document. The county social services office can explain what is required, but families often work with an elder law attorney to set it up correctly. Once the trust is in place, the income deposited into it is typically used toward the cost of care, with Medicaid covering what remains.

faqs.question: Can my parent keep their house if it's worth more than $2,000?
faqs.answer: Yes. The home your parent lives in is excluded from the $2,000 asset limit entirely, regardless of its value. One vehicle is also excluded. The $2,000 limit applies only to countable assets such as bank account balances, CDs, stocks, and other liquid or financial resources. However, if your parent owns additional real property beyond their primary home, that property does count toward the limit.

faqs.question: My parent transferred money to family members recently. Does that affect eligibility?
faqs.answer: It can. MLTSS uses Medicaid's institutional long-term-care financial rules, which include a five-year look-back period. If your parent transferred assets for less than fair market value within the past five years, Medicaid may impose a period of ineligibility. The length of the penalty depends on the amount transferred. Do not make additional financial transfers before speaking with the county social services office or an elder law attorney.

faqs.question: My parent's income is over $2,982/month. Are they automatically disqualified?
faqs.answer: No. Income above the $2,982/month Medicaid long-term-care limit (2026) does not automatically end eligibility if a Qualified Income Trust (QIT) is established correctly. The QIT is a legal trust document where the excess income is deposited each month. Medicaid then treats the person as within the income limit. Ask the county social services office about the QIT process, and consider consulting an elder law attorney to set it up.

faqs.question: Can a family member apply on behalf of an aging parent?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member with legal authority can apply on behalf of a parent. You will need documentation of that authority, such as a durable power of attorney, guardianship order, or healthcare proxy. Bring those documents when you contact the county ADRC or submit the NJ FamilyCare application. Without documentation of legal authority, the county may require the applicant to participate directly in the process.

faqs.question: What happens after my parent enrolls? Can the care plan change as their needs change?
faqs.answer: Yes. After enrollment, the managed care organization assigns a care manager who conducts an initial assessment and develops a service plan. If your parent's condition changes, you can request a reassessment at any time. The care manager is your point of contact for adding, changing, or removing services. Keep the care manager informed of significant changes in your parent's health or living situation so the plan stays current.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for MLTSS and still receive other NJ Medicaid benefits at the same time?
faqs.answer: MLTSS is part of NJ FamilyCare, so enrollment generally includes NJ FamilyCare Plan A health coverage as well as long-term services. Your parent does not need to apply separately for those benefits; they are coordinated through the managed care organization. If your parent currently receives other Medicaid benefits, ask the county social services office how those will transition when MLTSS enrollment begins.

faqs.question: How long will it take to get services started after applying?
faqs.answer: There is no single fixed processing timeline for MLTSS. The process has two parts: the clinical screening (conducted by the county ADRC) and the financial eligibility determination (through the NJ FamilyCare application). Both must be completed before enrollment with a managed care plan can begin. Timing depends on how quickly documentation is gathered, how the county is currently processing applications, and how quickly the MCO can complete its own care assessment. Ask your county ADRC for current expected timelines when you begin.

faqs.question: My parent is in the hospital right now. Can we start the application from there?
faqs.answer: Yes, and starting from the hospital can be the fastest route. Ask to speak with the hospital's discharge planner or social worker and tell them your parent may need nursing-home-level care through MLTSS. Discharge planners are familiar with the MLTSS clinical screening process and can often initiate it before your parent leaves the hospital. Acting early can help avoid a gap in care at discharge.

programs.name: NJ FamilyCare Medicare Savings Programs
programs.tagline: If your parent is on Medicare with limited income, New Jersey may pay their Medicare premiums and other out-of-pocket costs, saving over $2,000 a year.

localEntities.name: County State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP)

programs.intro:
If your parent is enrolled in Medicare Part A and Part B and lives on a fixed income, New Jersey may pay some or all of their Medicare costs through the Medicare Savings Programs (MSP). Depending on their income, the state can cover the Medicare Part B premium (currently $185/month in 2026), and at the highest benefit tier, also cover deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. That adds up to more than $2,000 a year in savings for many families.

There are three tiers: QMB, SLMB, and QI-1. Each tier has a different income limit and covers different costs. QMB is the most generous and covers the broadest set of Medicare cost-sharing. SLMB and QI-1 focus on the Part B premium. All three tiers share the same asset limit and are administered through NJ FamilyCare.

This is not the same as full Medicaid. Your parent keeps their Medicare coverage; the state just steps in to pay costs Medicare would otherwise bill to them. To qualify, your parent must already be enrolled in both Medicare Part A and Part B, live in New Jersey, and meet the income and asset limits described below.

applicationGuide.summary: Apply online through NJSave at nj.gov, or call 1-800-701-0710 for help completing the application by phone.

steps.description: Confirm your parent's gross annual income against the tier limits: QMB (single $15,960/year, couple $21,640/year), SLMB (single $19,152/year, couple $25,968/year), QI-1 (single $21,546/year, couple $29,214/year). Check liquid assets: the limit is $9,950 for a single person and $14,910 for a couple. The home and one car do not count toward the asset limit.

steps.title: Get free in-person help through SHIP
steps.description: If the application feels complicated, your county's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) offers free one-on-one help. SHIP counselors can walk through the form with your parent and help identify which tier they qualify for. Contact 1-800-792-9745 to find your local SHIP office.

steps.title: Track your application and respond promptly
steps.description: After submitting, watch for any requests for additional documents. Responding quickly prevents delays. No specific statewide processing time has been published by NJ FamilyCare, so follow up if you have not heard back within 30 days.

faqs.question: My parent owns a home. Does that disqualify them from the asset limit?
faqs.answer: No. New Jersey specifically excludes the primary home and one car from the asset calculation. Only liquid assets and countable financial resources apply toward the $9,950 (single) or $14,910 (couple) limit. If your parent's only assets are their home and a modest savings account, they may still qualify.

faqs.question: My parent is close to but slightly above the income limit. Is there anything we can do?
faqs.answer: The income limits are fixed for each tier, so there is no formal spend-down process for the Medicare Savings Programs the way there is for full Medicaid. However, some income may not count in the calculation. Call 1-800-701-0710 to have a counselor review what income is counted; in some cases, deductions or exclusions apply.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent if they cannot complete the form themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or authorized representative can complete the NJSave application on behalf of the applicant. If you have legal authority such as power of attorney, mention that when you call 1-800-701-0710. SHIP counselors can also assist if you need in-person support.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for this and Extra Help for prescriptions at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is worth doing both in the same session. Enrollment in QMB, SLMB, or QI-1 may automatically qualify your parent for Extra Help (the Low Income Subsidy that reduces Medicare Part D drug costs). Ask about this when you call 1-800-701-0710 or when completing the NJSave application.

faqs.question: What does QMB actually cover day to day, and does my parent still get billed?
faqs.answer: Under QMB, Medicare providers are not allowed to bill your parent for Medicare cost-sharing, which includes deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. If your parent receives a bill from a provider while enrolled in QMB, they can dispute it. Call 1-800-701-0710 or contact your local SHIP office at 1-800-792-9745 if this happens.

faqs.question: How often does my parent need to renew, and what happens if they miss the renewal?
faqs.answer: NJ FamilyCare conducts periodic renewals for Medicare Savings Programs enrollment. The state will send a renewal notice; respond promptly with updated income and asset information to avoid a gap in coverage. If coverage lapses, your parent can reapply through NJSave at any time. There is no open enrollment window restriction.

faqs.question: My parent is in a Medicare Advantage plan, not original Medicare. Do they still qualify?
faqs.answer: Yes. Medicare Advantage plans still require Medicare Part A and Part B enrollment, and that enrollment is what the Medicare Savings Programs look at. If your parent meets the income and asset limits, the MSP can still pay their Part B premium and applicable cost-sharing regardless of whether they use original Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan.

faqs.question: Is there a waitlist for these programs?
faqs.answer: No waitlist applies to the Medicare Savings Programs in New Jersey. Eligibility is based on income and assets; if your parent qualifies, they are enrolled. Funding is subject to annual Congressional approval for the QI-1 tier specifically, but there is no queue to join for any tier.

programs.name: NJ SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: If your parent is on a fixed income in New Jersey, they may qualify for up to $298/month toward groceries loaded automatically onto a card they can use at most grocery stores.

programs.intro:
If your parent is 60 or older and living on Social Security, a pension, or other fixed income, they may qualify for NJ SNAP: a monthly grocery benefit loaded onto an EBT card they can use at most supermarkets and many farmers markets. For a one-person household, the monthly benefit ranges from $95 to $298. For a two-person household, it ranges from $95 to $546.

Seniors often assume SNAP is only for low-income families with children. That is not the case. In New Jersey, households that include someone age 60 or older or a person with a disability are treated differently under SNAP rules: they may qualify even if their gross monthly income is above the standard limit that applies to other households. If your parent was turned away before or never applied because they thought they earned too much, it may be worth checking again.

The program is run statewide through New Jersey's county social service agencies. Your parent applies once, completes a phone or in-person interview with their county, and if approved, receives benefits within 30 days. Households in urgent financial situations may receive benefits within 7 days. The card works like a debit card at checkout; the cashier does not need to know it is a government benefit.

applicationGuide.summary: The fastest way to start is the online application at NJHelps.gov, which takes 20 to 40 minutes; a county interview follows and most cases are decided within 30 days.

steps.title: Gather basic information before you start
steps.description: Before opening the application, collect your parent's monthly income sources (Social Security award letter, pension statement), proof of New Jersey address, and basic household information. You do not need to have every document in hand to submit the application, but having income figures ready speeds it up.

steps.title: Submit the application online at NJHelps.gov
steps.description: Go to NJHelps.gov (also accessible at MyNJHelps.gov) and complete the NJ SNAP application. The form takes roughly 20 to 40 minutes. You can save and return if needed. Submit electronically when complete. If you prefer to apply in person, go to your county's social services agency; call 2-1-1 to find the office nearest you.

steps.title: Complete the required interview with your county
steps.description: After submission, your county social services agency will schedule an interview. This is required; benefits cannot be approved without it. The interview is typically by phone and covers your parent's income, household situation, and expenses. Some counties also offer in-person interviews. Your county will contact you to schedule.

steps.title: Submit verification documents the county requests
steps.description: After or during the interview, the county will tell you exactly which documents they need. Submit everything they ask for as quickly as possible, because the 30-day processing clock can be affected by missing paperwork. Documents are typically submitted to your county office in person, by mail, or by fax depending on the county.

steps.title: Receive your EBT card and start using benefits
steps.description: If approved, your parent will receive a Families First EBT card in the mail. Benefits are loaded to the card monthly. The card works like a debit card at most grocery stores and many farmers markets in New Jersey. It cannot be used to buy alcohol, tobacco, vitamins, or prepared hot foods.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Most cases are decided within 30 days of application. Households in urgent situations (very low income, minimal resources, or facing immediate food hardship) may qualify for expedited benefits within 7 days.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is in an urgent situation, ask specifically about expedited processing when you call or during the interview. Not everyone qualifies, but if they do, benefits can arrive within 7 days instead of 30.

County offices administer cases, so interview scheduling, acceptable document formats, and processing speed can vary. If one county's office is slow to schedule, ask whether there is a SNAP Navigator who can help move the process along.

contentSections.title: What the EBT card can and cannot buy
contentSections.body: The Families First EBT card works like a debit card at most grocery stores and many farmers markets. Your parent can use it to buy bread, meat, produce, dairy, canned goods, and most packaged foods. They cannot use it to buy alcohol, tobacco, vitamins and supplements, pet food, or prepared hot foods (like a rotisserie chicken that is sold hot). There is no cash-back option. The card balance carries over month to month if not fully used.

contentSections.title: Asset limits: what we know and what we do not
contentSections.body: SNAP does review household resources (cash, checking and savings account balances, and similar liquid assets) as part of eligibility. However, the official New Jersey SNAP materials do not publish a specific dollar limit for asset tests. Certain resources are excluded under federal SNAP rules, including the home your parent lives in. Because the official state source does not publish a full asset table, we are not stating a specific limit here. When your parent completes the county interview, the caseworker will ask about resources and explain what counts. If you want to understand this before the interview, ask the county caseworker directly.

faqs.question: My parent's income is above the limit in the table. Are they definitely ineligible?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Households that include someone age 60 or older or a person with a disability may qualify under different income rules than the standard gross income limits. The limits shown in the table above apply to most households, but seniors and people with disabilities can sometimes qualify above those figures. The only way to know for certain is to apply or ask your county agency directly. Do not assume a denial based on the standard table.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly parent, or do they have to do it themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or other authorized representative can apply on behalf of an elderly or disabled person. You can complete the NJHelps.gov application on their behalf and participate in the county interview as their representative. You will need to be identified as the authorized representative during the application. The county can explain the representative process if you call before applying.

faqs.question: My parent already gets SSI or Medicaid. Do they automatically get SNAP?
faqs.answer: No. SNAP is a separate application in New Jersey and is not automatic even for people who receive SSI, Medicaid, or other government benefits. Your parent must apply through NJHelps.gov or their county office and complete an interview. That said, receiving SSI or Medicaid may simplify some parts of the eligibility review.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for SNAP and NJ LIHEAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. SNAP and LIHEAP are separate programs with separate applications, but nothing prevents applying to both at the same time. Applying to both is worth doing because receiving certain utility assistance can actually increase the SNAP benefit amount through a deduction in the benefit calculation. Start both applications in the same period so the LIHEAP enrollment can be documented when SNAP eligibility is reviewed.

faqs.question: How long does approval take, and can we get faster help if my parent has no food now?
faqs.answer: Most cases are approved within 30 days. If your parent has very little money and an immediate need for food, ask specifically about expedited processing when you contact the county. Qualifying households can receive benefits within 7 days. Not everyone qualifies for expedited processing, but the county caseworker will screen for it. Tell them about the urgency at the start of the conversation.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's income or household situation changes after they are enrolled?
faqs.answer: Your parent is required to report certain changes to their county agency, such as a significant increase in income or a change in household size. Changes can affect the benefit amount or eligibility. At each recertification (the periodic renewal review), the county will reassess the full situation. If income drops or a new expense arises between renewals, your parent can also report changes proactively, which may increase their benefit.

faqs.question: My parent was denied SNAP before. Is it worth applying again?
faqs.answer: It may be. SNAP income limits are adjusted annually, and households with a member age 60 or older are evaluated under different rules than standard households. If the previous denial was based on income and your parent is 60 or older, the standard income table may not have been the correct standard. A new application will be evaluated under current rules. There is no penalty for reapplying.

faqs.question: Does my parent's home count against them in the asset test?
faqs.answer: Under federal SNAP rules, the home a person lives in is excluded from the asset test. It does not count as a resource. The NJ SNAP materials do not publish a full list of what is counted or excluded beyond this, so if your parent has savings accounts, investment accounts, or other assets, the county caseworker will review those during the interview and explain what counts in their specific situation.

programs.name: NJ LIHEAP (Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: If your parent pays a heating or cooling bill in New Jersey and earns below a certain income, they may receive up to $4,878 toward energy costs this season.

localEntities.name: Authorized local community action agencies in each county
New Jersey Energy Assistance Hotline: 1-800-510-3102

programs.intro:
If your parent is on a fixed income and struggling to pay a heating or cooling bill in New Jersey, LIHEAP can help. The program provides a direct payment toward home energy costs, up to $4,878 per household including any emergency or repair payments. The benefit goes directly to the utility company or fuel supplier, so your parent never has to manage a reimbursement.

This is not a senior-only program. Any New Jersey household that meets the income limit qualifies, including households where your parent lives with you. A single person can earn up to $2,518 per month (gross) and still qualify for FY2026. If your parent rents and heat is included in the rent, they may still qualify, as long as their lease shows they are responsible for that energy cost.

The application season runs October 1 through June 30 each year, and funding is limited. Applying early in the season reduces the risk of funds running out. You can apply online at energyassistance.nj.gov or by calling 1-800-510-3102 to be connected with your county's community action agency.
programs.savingsRange: Up to $4,878 per household per program year (FY2026 maximum, including standard payments, emergency assistance, and emergency furnace repair payments). Average heating awards run approximately $360 and average medically necessary cooling awards approximately $300, but individual amounts vary by household circumstances.
programs.savingsSource: NJ Department of Community Affairs LIHEAP program materials and FY2026 income limit table published at nj.gov/dca/dhcr/offices/hea.shtml. The $4,878 figure is the state-published maximum. Averages of $360 (heating) and $300 (medically necessary cooling) are cited in NJ utility program materials.

steps.title: Confirm the season is open
steps.description: LIHEAP accepts applications October 1 through June 30 only, and funding is limited. If you are applying after February, call 1-800-510-3102 to confirm funds are still available in your county before gathering documents.

steps.title: Gather your documents before you start
steps.description: You will need proof of New Jersey residency, proof of income for all household members, and your most recent utility bill or lease showing you are responsible for heating costs. Incomplete applications are the most common reason for delays. Having everything ready before you open the application saves significant time.

steps.title: Apply online or by phone
steps.description: Online: go to energyassistance.nj.gov and complete the Home Energy/USF/Weatherization Program Application. This is the same combined form used for LIHEAP and USF (Universal Service Fund). Phone: call 1-800-510-3102 to reach the NJ Energy Assistance Hotline, which will connect you with the community action agency serving your county.

steps.title: Submit to your county community action agency
steps.description: If you applied online, your application routes to the authorized community action agency in your county. If you applied by phone or in person, that agency handles processing. Processing timelines depend on county agency workload and how complete your application is. There is no single statewide processing guarantee.

steps.title: Check your application status
steps.description: After submitting, you can check your status at nj.gov/dca/dcaid. If the agency needs additional documents, respond promptly; missing documentation is the most common reason applications stall.

steps.title: Benefit is paid directly to the utility or fuel supplier
steps.description: If approved, the payment goes directly to your parent's utility company or fuel supplier. Your parent will receive a notice. No reimbursement process or check to manage.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Processing time is not guaranteed by the state; it varies by county agency workload and application completeness. Applying early in the season (October through December) typically results in faster processing than applying in spring when demand peaks and funds may be running low.
applicationGuide.waitlist: There is no formal statewide waitlist. However, LIHEAP is funded seasonally and accepted while funds last. Applying late in the season (after April) carries a real risk of funding exhaustion before your application is processed.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent has received a utility shutoff notice, call 1-800-510-3102 immediately and say there is an active disconnection notice. Emergency assistance may be available with faster processing. Do not wait to gather every document before calling in a crisis.

The LIHEAP application in New Jersey is the same combined form as the USF (Universal Service Fund) and Weatherization applications. Completing one form makes you considered for all three programs. USF and LIHEAP are different programs with different benefits; receiving one does not guarantee the other.

If your parent lives with you and the household income combined exceeds the limit, they will not qualify. Income is counted on a household basis, not per individual. If your parent lives alone or with another low-income person, the single or two-person income limit applies.

An older adult in assisted living or a care facility where the facility pays all utilities is unlikely to qualify, because the household must be responsible for the energy costs. Call 1-800-510-3102 to confirm eligibility before starting the application.

NJ Low Income Household Water Assistance Program (LIHWAP): similar income-based assistance for water and wastewater bills

contentSections.title: Heat included in rent still counts
contentSections.body: A common reason families skip this application is the assumption that because the landlord pays the utility company directly, the tenant does not qualify. New Jersey LIHEAP allows households where heating costs are included in rent to apply, as long as the lease documents that the tenant is responsible for those costs. If your parent's rent includes heat, check the lease and apply.

contentSections.title: The application closes June 30 and funding runs out before that
contentSections.body: LIHEAP is not open year-round. The season runs October 1 through June 30, and New Jersey distributes a fixed pool of federal funds on a first-come basis. If you are reading this in the spring, call 1-800-510-3102 to confirm funds remain available in your county before investing time in the application.

contentSections.title: FY2026 Income Limits by Household Size
contentSections.description: These are the gross monthly income limits for LIHEAP eligibility in New Jersey for FY2026, based on 60% of State Median Income. All household members' income counts.

faqs.question: My parent lives with me. Does my income count against their eligibility?
faqs.answer: Yes. LIHEAP is a household-based program, not an individual benefit. Every person living in the home counts as part of the household, and all household members' gross income is combined to determine eligibility. If the combined household income exceeds the limit for your household size, no one in the home qualifies. The limit for a household of two is $3,291 per month (FY2026); for three people it is $4,064 per month. If your parent lives alone, only their income counts.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my aging parent?
faqs.answer: Yes. An authorized representative, including an adult child acting as caregiver, can apply on behalf of a household member who cannot apply themselves. You will need to provide your own identification and documentation showing you are acting on their behalf. Call 1-800-510-3102 or apply at energyassistance.nj.gov to start the process.

faqs.question: My parent's landlord pays the electric bill directly. Can they still qualify?
faqs.answer: Possibly. If the lease or rental agreement shows that heating costs are included in the rent, the household may still qualify even if the tenant never writes a check directly to the utility. The key is that the lease must document the tenant's responsibility for those energy costs. Bring the lease to the application. If the lease is unclear, call 1-800-510-3102 before assuming your parent does not qualify.

faqs.question: Is there a savings or asset limit? Does my parent need to spend down bank accounts first?
faqs.answer: No. New Jersey LIHEAP does not have an asset test based on the official program materials. There is no savings limit, no bank balance requirement, and no spend-down. Eligibility is based on household gross income and responsibility for home energy costs, not on how much money your parent has in savings.

faqs.question: My parent got a shutoff notice. Is it too late to apply?
faqs.answer: No. Call 1-800-510-3102 immediately and tell them there is an active disconnection notice. LIHEAP includes emergency assistance provisions that may allow for faster action. New Jersey utility companies are also required to check for energy assistance program eligibility before disconnecting a customer. Do not wait to gather every document before calling in a crisis.

faqs.question: Can my parent receive LIHEAP and USF at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the application is the same combined form. LIHEAP provides a one-time seasonal payment toward energy costs. USF (Universal Service Fund) provides an ongoing monthly discount on electric and gas bills for income-eligible households. They are separate programs with separate benefits. Completing the combined Home Energy/USF/Weatherization Application at energyassistance.nj.gov submits your parent for consideration for all three at once.

faqs.question: My parent needs help with summer cooling, not heating. Does LIHEAP cover that?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP primarily covers heating costs, but New Jersey does offer assistance for medically necessary cooling. To qualify for cooling assistance, your parent's physician must document that the medical condition requires air conditioning. Average cooling awards run approximately $300, based on NJ utility program materials, though individual amounts vary. Apply through the same portal at energyassistance.nj.gov and note the medical cooling need.

faqs.question: What if we apply and the funds run out before a decision is made?
faqs.answer: There is no formal statewide waitlist. If funding is exhausted before your application is processed, the application may not result in a benefit for that program year. This is the practical risk of applying late in the season. Applying early, ideally between October and December, significantly reduces this risk. If you are applying in spring, call 1-800-510-3102 to confirm funds are still available in your county before you start.

programs.name: New Jersey PACE (Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly)
programs.tagline: If your parent needs nursing-home-level care but wants to stay home, PACE covers everything: doctor visits, prescriptions, dental, home care, and transportation, all coordinated by one team.

localEntities.name: Local PACE organizations serving the applicant's county or region
New Jersey Division of Aging Services PACE page for statewide program information

programs.intro:
If your parent qualifies for nursing home care but you want them to stay in their own home or yours, New Jersey PACE may be the most comprehensive program available to them. PACE replaces the fragmented system of separate doctors, specialists, home aides, and pharmacies with a single interdisciplinary team that manages all of your parent's care. That team handles primary care, dental care, prescriptions, home care, adult day health services, and transportation to every appointment.

Eligibility is based on clinical need and geography, not income or assets. Your parent must be 55 or older, require nursing home level of care (meaning a clinical assessment finds they need daily help with bathing, dressing, medication management, or similar tasks), and be able to live safely in the community with PACE support at the time they enroll. They must also live inside the service area of a local PACE organization. New Jersey has expanded PACE coverage across all 21 counties, but the specific provider and service boundaries still matter.

For families navigating Medicare and Medicaid, PACE is designed to work with both. If your parent has Medicaid, PACE is typically covered at no cost to them. If they have Medicare only, or both Medicare and Medicaid, PACE replaces most of what those programs would separately cover. Some participants who do not qualify for Medicaid pay a monthly premium. The NJ Division of Aging Services is the state authority for this program.
programs.savingsSource: Free service: PACE is covered by Medicare and Medicaid for eligible participants. Costs for those paying privately vary by local PACE organization and are not published statewide.

structuredEligibility.functionalRequirement: Your parent must meet nursing facility level of care, meaning a clinical assessment finds they need daily assistance with activities like bathing, dressing, eating, transferring, toileting, or managing medications. This is determined by the PACE organization's interdisciplinary team, not by the family.
otherRequirements: Must live within the service area of a New Jersey PACE organization at the time of enrollment
Must be able to live safely in the community with PACE support (cannot require 24-hour institutional supervision that PACE cannot provide)

PACE is available to those on Medicare, Medicaid, both, or neither (private pay). Medicaid or Medicare enrollment is not itself a requirement for PACE eligibility, but it determines how costs are covered.

steps.description: Go to nj.gov/humanservices/doas/services/l-p/pace/ to find the PACE organizations operating in New Jersey. Your parent must live within a provider's coverage area to enroll. If you are unsure, call the NJ Division of Aging Services at (609) 943-3343 and ask which PACE organization, if any, serves your parent's zip code.

steps.title: Contact the local PACE organization directly
steps.description: Once you have identified the PACE provider for your parent's area, call them to request an enrollment inquiry. Each organization handles its own intake. They will ask about your parent's age, current care needs, and living situation to determine whether a clinical assessment makes sense.

steps.title: Gather key documents before the assessment call
steps.description: You do not need everything at the first call, but having proof of age, proof of NJ residence, and a current medication list ready will speed things up. If your parent has Medicare or Medicaid, have those card numbers or letters on hand.

steps.title: Complete the clinical eligibility assessment
steps.description: A PACE interdisciplinary team will conduct an assessment, typically at the PACE center or at your parent's home, to determine whether they meet nursing facility level of care and can safely live in the community with PACE support. This is the core eligibility gate.

steps.title: Review the enrollment agreement and begin services
steps.description: If your parent is found eligible, the PACE organization will walk you through an enrollment agreement covering how costs are handled (through Medicaid, Medicare, or private pay). Once signed, the PACE team takes over coordinating all care.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No statewide processing timeline is published. Timeline depends on the local PACE organization's assessment schedule.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No statewide waitlist has been identified in official NJ PACE materials. Availability depends on whether a PACE organization is operating in your parent's service area and whether they have capacity. Ask the local provider directly.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is being discharged from a hospital or rehabilitation facility, tell the discharge planner you are interested in PACE. They can often initiate the referral faster than an outside call.

PACE replaces Medicare and Medicaid as the primary payer for all covered services once your parent enrolls. Your parent will generally need to use the PACE team's network of providers rather than keeping their existing doctors, unless the PACE team arranges otherwise.

If your parent does not have Medicaid and is not yet enrolled, it may be worth applying for NJ FamilyCare (New Jersey's Medicaid program) at the same time you pursue PACE, since Medicaid coverage eliminates out-of-pocket costs for PACE participants.
PACE enrollment is voluntary. Your parent must agree to participate and can disenroll at any time, at which point their Medicare and Medicaid coverage reverts to the standard fee-for-service model.

contentSections.title: What PACE actually replaces
contentSections.body: Most families managing a parent's care are coordinating between a primary care doctor, one or more specialists, a home health agency, a pharmacy, and transportation services. Each of those involves separate scheduling, separate billing, and separate conversations. Because PACE covers all of those under one program, your parent's entire care is managed by a single interdisciplinary team. That team includes doctors, nurses, social workers, therapists, and home care aides who communicate with each other directly. You no longer have to be the coordinator.

contentSections.title: How costs work
contentSections.body:
If your parent has both Medicare and Medicaid, PACE is typically available at no cost to them. If they have Medicare only, PACE covers the same services but may charge a monthly premium for the Medicaid portion of benefits. If they have neither Medicare nor Medicaid and choose to pay privately, the PACE organization sets a monthly rate. No statewide private-pay rate is published; contact the local PACE organization for their current figures.

Once enrolled, your parent cannot use Medicare or Medicaid to pay for services outside the PACE network, except in a genuine emergency. This is the trade-off: comprehensive, coordinated care in exchange for using the PACE team's providers.

faqs.question: My parent wants to stay home. Will PACE force them to go to a day center?
faqs.answer: Adult day health services are part of PACE, and many participants attend a PACE center several days a week. However, PACE also provides home care. The interdisciplinary team builds a care plan around your parent's needs and preferences. The goal of PACE is to keep your parent living in the community, not to move them to a facility.

faqs.question: Can my parent keep their current doctors if they enroll in PACE?
faqs.answer: Generally, no. Enrolling in PACE means your parent's care shifts to the PACE organization's interdisciplinary team. PACE becomes the primary manager of all medical and social services. If your parent has a long-standing specialist relationship they want to preserve, ask the local PACE organization during the assessment whether that provider can be incorporated into the care plan. It depends on the specific organization.

faqs.question: My parent has Medicare but not Medicaid. Can they still join PACE?
faqs.answer: Yes. Medicare alone does not disqualify a person from PACE. If your parent has Medicare only, PACE will cover the Medicaid portion of services but may charge a monthly premium for it. The clinical eligibility requirements, age 55 or older, nursing facility level of care, and safe community living at enrollment, remain the same regardless of insurance status. Contact the local PACE organization for their current premium rates.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's condition gets worse after they enroll?
faqs.answer: The PACE interdisciplinary team continuously reassesses participants and adjusts care plans as needs change. If your parent eventually requires nursing home placement, PACE can arrange and cover that too, because nursing facility care is a covered PACE service. PACE is designed to follow a person's clinical trajectory, not to drop them when their needs increase.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent if they cannot manage the process themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you hold a health care proxy, durable power of attorney, or court-ordered guardianship for your parent, you can initiate the PACE inquiry and participate in the enrollment process on their behalf. Bring a copy of whatever legal document authorizes you to act for your parent when you contact the PACE organization.

faqs.question: What if there is no PACE provider in my parent's area?
faqs.answer: New Jersey has expanded PACE to all 21 counties, but coverage still depends on a specific PACE organization operating in your parent's zip code. If no provider currently serves that area, New Jersey's Global Options for Long-Term Care Medicaid waiver and the NJ Statewide Respite Care Program may offer some of the same home and community-based services. Call the NJ Division of Aging Services at (609) 943-3343 to discuss alternatives.

faqs.question: Can my parent leave PACE if they change their mind?
faqs.answer: Yes. PACE enrollment is voluntary and your parent can disenroll at any time. When they leave PACE, their Medicare and Medicaid coverage automatically reverts to the standard fee-for-service arrangement. There is no penalty for disenrolling, but they will need to re-establish care with outside providers after leaving.

faqs.question: Does PACE cover dental care and prescriptions, or just medical visits?
faqs.answer: Yes. New Jersey PACE explicitly covers dental care and prescriptions in addition to primary care, specialist visits, home care, adult day health services, and transportation to appointments. Because PACE manages all covered services under one program, your parent does not pay separately for each type of service the way they would with standard Medicare or Medicaid.

programs.name: New Jersey Family Caregiver Support Program
programs.tagline: If you're caring for a parent 60 or older in New Jersey, this program connects you to free counseling, respite options, and local support, with no income limit to get started.

localEntities.name: Local Area Agencies on Aging (AAA) in each county
Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC)
NJ 211 caregiver navigation line

programs.intro:
If you are helping an aging parent stay home, this program is built for you, not your parent. The New Jersey Family Caregiver Support Program provides free services to family caregivers through local Area Agencies on Aging (AAA) in every New Jersey county. That can include caregiver counseling, information about respite options, help navigating local services, and connections to support groups. There is no income test to access basic services; middle-income families qualify alongside those with the greatest financial need.

The program covers caregivers of adults 60 and older, and caregivers of people of any age diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. You do not need to be related by blood. You do not need a Medicaid case open. This is a state-funded caregiver support program, not a Medicaid benefit, so different rules apply.

Because services are delivered locally through county AAA and ADRC offices, what is available to you depends on where you live. Some counties have more respite resources and support groups than others. The first step is contacting your local AAA or calling 1-877-222-3737 to find out exactly what is offered in your area.

No income limit to access basic services
Available statewide through your county's Area Agency on Aging
