Eligibility is based on the care recipient's age or diagnosis, not the caregiver's income or assets.
Priority for certain services is given to caregivers with the greatest social and economic need, which means limited services may be directed to those families first.

applicationGuide.summary: Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach the NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection, which will connect you to your county's AAA for a needs assessment and next steps.

steps.title: Call the statewide ADRC line
steps.description: Call 1-877-222-3737. This is the New Jersey Aging and Disability Resource Connection line. Tell the counselor you are a family caregiver looking for caregiver support services. They will identify your county's Area Agency on Aging and connect you or give you the direct contact.

steps.title: Speak with your county AAA
steps.description: Your county's Area Agency on Aging conducts an intake conversation to understand your caregiving situation, your parent's needs, and what support would help most. Gather basic information beforehand: your parent's age, any diagnoses, and a brief description of the help you are currently providing.

steps.title: Get matched to local services
steps.description: Based on your conversation, the AAA will tell you which caregiver support services are available in your county. This may include counseling, caregiver training, support groups, respite referrals, or help navigating other programs. Specific offerings vary by county.

steps.title: Follow up as your situation changes
steps.description: There is no fixed enrollment period. Contact your county AAA again if your parent's care needs increase, if a crisis arises, or if you need a different type of support. You can also call NJ 211 (dial 2-1-1) at any time for general referrals to caregiver resources.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No official statewide processing timeline is published. Your county AAA sets its own intake schedule.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No statewide waitlist exists for this program. Availability of specific services (such as respite) can vary by county; ask your local AAA directly about current wait times for any service you need.
applicationGuide.tip: When you call, be ready to describe your current caregiving situation in plain terms: how many hours a day you help, what tasks you handle, and what is hardest right now. The more specific you are, the faster the AAA can match you to the right support.

documentsNeeded: Your parent's date of birth or age (to confirm they are 60 or older)
Your parent's diagnosis, if they have Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia (required if under 60)
Your contact information: name, phone number, and county of residence
A brief description of the caregiving you currently provide (tasks, hours, living situation)
Any relevant medical or functional information about your parent that helps describe the level of care needed

contacts.label: NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC)
contacts.description: The primary entry point for caregiver support services statewide. Counselors can connect you to your county's Area Agency on Aging and explain what services are available near you.
contacts.hours: Contact the line for current hours

contacts.label: NJ 211 Caregiver Line
contacts.description: General helpline that can refer you to local caregiver resources and connect you to the right county office if you are unsure where to start. This line transfers rather than handling program intake directly.

applicationNotes: This is a caregiver support program, not a Medicaid program. Your parent does not need to be on Medicaid, and there is no income or asset test for basic services. Middle-income families are welcome.
If you are in a caregiving crisis (sudden hospitalization, caregiver burnout, no backup plan), tell the AAA that clearly when you call. Some counties prioritize crisis situations for faster intake.

Because services are delivered locally, what is available in Bergen County may differ from what is available in Cumberland County. If you feel your needs are not being met, ask whether adjacent county AAAs serve your area or have programs yours does not.

This program can run alongside Medicaid-based programs. If your parent is also on Medicaid or you are exploring Medicaid home care, caregiver support services here can supplement, not replace, those benefits.
relatedPrograms: NJ Global Options for Long-Term Care (Medicaid home and community-based waiver)
NJ Personal Preference Program (Medicaid self-directed home care)
NJ SHIP (State Health Insurance Assistance Program, free Medicare counseling)
NJ Respite Coalition caregiver respite services

contentSections.title: This program is for you, the caregiver, not just your parent.
contentSections.body: Most government programs require your parent to apply and qualify. This one is different. You, as the caregiver, are the primary beneficiary. The services (counseling, training, support groups, respite referrals) are designed to help you keep doing what you are doing without burning out. Your parent's age or diagnosis determines whether you are eligible, but the program exists to support you.

contentSections.title: What services can you actually get?
contentSections.body: The program does not pay a fixed cash benefit or guarantee a specific package of services. Instead, your county AAA assesses your situation and connects you to what is available locally. Across the state, that typically includes: caregiver counseling and support groups, information about local respite care options (temporary relief so you can take a break), training to help you provide safer, more effective care, and help navigating other programs your parent may qualify for. The specific services and their availability depend on your county. No two county AAAs operate identically.

contentSections.title: Who gets priority when services are limited?
contentSections.body: The program is open to all family caregivers meeting the basic criteria, regardless of income. But when a county has limited capacity for a specific service (like in-home respite), priority goes to caregivers with the greatest social and economic need. That means a middle-income family may wait longer for some services than a lower-income family in the same county. Ask your AAA directly how prioritization works for any service you are requesting.

faqs.question: My parent is 58 and does not have dementia. Can I still get help through this program?
faqs.answer: No. The program covers caregivers of adults who are 60 or older, or of people with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia at any age. If your parent is under 60 and does not have a qualifying dementia diagnosis, this program does not apply. Contact NJ 211 (dial 2-1-1) for referrals to other caregiver resources that may serve younger care recipients.

faqs.question: Our household income is too high for most programs. Can we still apply?
faqs.answer: Yes. There is no income test for basic access to caregiver support services under this program. Middle-income families qualify. Priority for some services goes to those with the greatest financial or social need, so you may wait longer for certain supports, but you are not disqualified. Call 1-877-222-3737 to start.

faqs.question: Does my parent have to be living with me to qualify?
faqs.answer: The program does not require that you live with your parent. What matters is that you are providing care to an adult 60 or older, or a person with Alzheimer's or a related dementia. If you are managing their care from a distance or visiting regularly to help, you can still contact your county AAA to discuss what support is available.

faqs.question: What is the difference between this program and Medicaid home care?
faqs.answer: They are completely separate. Medicaid home care programs (like NJ Global Options) pay for services provided to your parent and require your parent to meet Medicaid income and functional eligibility rules. The NJ Family Caregiver Support Program is a state-funded program that provides support to you as the caregiver, with no income test and no Medicaid enrollment required. You can use both at the same time if your parent qualifies for Medicaid.

faqs.question: How long will it take to actually get help after I call?
faqs.answer: No statewide processing timeline is published for this program. Intake speed and service availability depend on your county's AAA. Ask directly when you call 1-877-222-3737 how long their current intake process takes and whether there is a wait for specific services like respite.

faqs.question: Can I get respite care paid for through this program?
faqs.answer: Respite care (temporary relief so you can take a break) is one of the supports this program may help you access. However, it is not a guaranteed cash payment. Your county AAA will tell you whether funded respite options exist locally and whether there is a waitlist. Ask your AAA specifically about respite when you call.

faqs.question: My sibling and I both help care for our mother. Can we both get caregiver support?
faqs.answer: Yes. The program serves family caregivers, and more than one person can be involved in a care situation. Contact your county AAA at 1-877-222-3737 to discuss the situation. The AAA will assess what is most useful given the full caregiving picture.

faqs.question: What if my needs change after I start receiving services?
faqs.answer: Contact your county AAA again. There is no fixed enrollment period and no requirement to wait for a renewal cycle. If your parent's condition worsens, if a hospitalization occurs, or if your own capacity to provide care changes, the AAA can reassess and connect you to different or additional supports.

programs.name: New Jersey Home Delivered Meals
programs.tagline: If your parent is 60+ and homebound, they may qualify for a hot meal delivered to their door five days a week, at no cost, through their county's aging services office.

localEntities.name: Local Area Agencies on Aging
County senior services or nutrition program offices
County Meals on Wheels providers

programs.intro:
If your parent is 60 or older, unable to cook for themselves, and doesn't have anyone at home to prepare meals, New Jersey's Home Delivered Meals program can arrange for a hot meal to be delivered to their door, typically five days a week. There is no statewide income limit. The program is not means-tested the way food stamps are; eligibility is based on your parent's functional situation, not their bank account.

The program is funded under the Older Americans Act and administered county by county through local Area Agencies on Aging. That means the specific delivery schedule, the intake process, and the paperwork your parent needs will depend on where they live. Most counties deliver on weekdays only, so this is not a seven-day solution on its own. A spouse living in the same home may also qualify for a meal if the primary participant is approved.

Approval is not automatic after one phone call. Every application requires a needs assessment, which is a conversation with a county staff member about your parent's daily functioning and what support they already have at home. Plan for that step before your parent's first delivery. The fastest way to get started is to contact your county's Area Agency on Aging directly.

summary: Homebound (unable to leave home without difficulty)
No one available at home to prepare meals
structuredEligibility.functionalRequirement: Your parent must be homebound (meaning they cannot easily leave home on their own) and unable to prepare their own meals. They must also lack a family member, friend, neighbor, or paid caregiver who is available to cook for them. A county staff member will conduct a needs assessment to confirm these conditions before approving services.
otherRequirements: Must reside in the county where they apply (some counties require this)
Spouse living in the same home may also qualify for a meal if the primary participant is approved
Some counties require a doctor's note or medical documentation of homebound status
No statewide income limit; financial need may affect priority if county demand is high

applicationGuide.summary: Call your county's Area Agency on Aging to start; they will conduct a brief needs assessment by phone and tell you what documents your county requires.

steps.title: Find your county's Area Agency on Aging
steps.description: New Jersey has county-level offices that run this program. Visit the NJ Division of Aging Services directory at nj.gov/humanservices/doas/home/ or call the NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 (Monday through Friday, 8am to 8pm) to get your county's direct number.

steps.title: Call and describe your parent's situation
steps.description: Tell the county office that your parent is 60 or older, homebound, and cannot prepare meals. They will screen your parent over the phone and tell you whether a full needs assessment is needed and what paperwork your county requires. Have your parent's date of birth and address ready.

steps.title: Complete the needs assessment
steps.description: A county staff member will conduct a formal assessment, either by phone or in person, to confirm your parent's homebound status, their ability to prepare food, and whether anyone else in the home can help. This step is required; services cannot start without it.

steps.title: Submit any required documents
steps.description: Some counties ask for a doctor's note confirming homebound status, proof of age, and proof of county residency. Requirements vary. Ask your county contact exactly what they need so you can submit everything at once and avoid delays.

steps.title: Wait for approval and first delivery
steps.description: Processing time varies by county. There is no published statewide timeline. Ask your county contact how long approval typically takes and whether there is a waitlist. Once approved, the county will schedule your parent's first delivery and tell you which days meals will arrive.

applicationGuide.processingTime: No statewide processing time is published. Timing varies by county; ask your county's Area Agency on Aging for a realistic estimate after the needs assessment.
applicationGuide.waitlist: No statewide waitlist policy is published. Some counties have waiting periods when demand is high. Ask your county office directly when you call.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is being discharged from a hospital or rehab facility and needs meals at home right away, tell the county that when you call. Some counties can expedite the assessment for post-discharge situations.

documentsNeeded: Proof of age (birth certificate, passport, or government-issued ID showing date of birth)
Proof of county residency, if required by your county (utility bill, lease, or official mail showing your parent's address)
Doctor's note or letter confirming homebound status and inability to prepare meals, if your county requests it
Completed county application form (your county's Area Agency on Aging will provide this)
Information about who else is in the household and whether anyone can prepare meals (you will be asked this during the needs assessment)

contacts.label: NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection
contacts.description: Call to get your county's Area Agency on Aging number and start the process. Staff can connect you to the right county office for your parent's address.

contacts.label: NJ Division of Aging Services
contacts.description: State-level office for general program questions. For applications, you will be directed to your county's local office.

applicationNotes: There is no income limit for this program. Do not assume your parent earns too much to qualify; the eligibility test is about homebound status and the ability to prepare meals, not finances.
If your parent's county has a waitlist, ask whether financial need or medical urgency affects priority. Some counties prioritize applicants with greater need when demand exceeds capacity.
A spouse living in the same home may also receive a meal, but this is not automatic. Ask about it specifically when you call, as not all counties extend this to every household member.
relatedPrograms: NJ Congregate Meals (senior center dining programs for those who can leave home)
NJ SNAP Food Assistance (monthly grocery benefit for low-income older adults)
NJ Personal Preference Program (self-directed home care for Medicaid-eligible seniors)
NJ Community Choice Counseling (free help exploring in-home care options)

contentSections.heading: No income limit
contentSections.body: Many families skip this program assuming their parent earns too much. There is no statewide income test. Eligibility is based on your parent's physical situation: are they homebound, can they cook, and is there someone else at home to help? If the answer points to no, they likely qualify regardless of income.

contentSections.heading: What the program does and does not cover
contentSections.body: Most counties deliver one hot meal per weekday, usually five days a week. This program is not designed to cover all meals for the week. It will not replace weekend meals, and it does not provide groceries or a meal stipend. If your parent needs more comprehensive food support, SNAP may cover the gaps for lower-income households. If your parent can leave home safely, congregate meal programs at local senior centers are another option and often have less paperwork.

faqs.question: My parent has some savings. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: No. There is no asset limit and no income limit for New Jersey's Home Delivered Meals program. The program does not look at savings, investments, or income. Eligibility is based entirely on your parent's functional situation: are they homebound, can they prepare their own meals, and is there anyone at home to help them? Financial situation only comes into play in some counties if demand exceeds supply and staff need to prioritize applicants.

faqs.question: What if my parent has family nearby? Does that automatically disqualify them?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but it is a factor the needs assessment will explore. The program requires that no family member, friend, neighbor, or paid caregiver is available to prepare meals. If you live nearby but work full-time and cannot cook for your parent daily, explain that during the assessment. The county will evaluate availability, not just physical proximity.

faqs.question: How long will it take before the first meal is delivered?
faqs.answer: There is no published statewide timeline. Processing depends on your county's current caseload and whether there is a waitlist. Some counties can start services within a few weeks of the assessment; others may take longer. Ask your county's Area Agency on Aging for a realistic estimate when you call. If your parent is being discharged from a hospital, mention that; some counties can move faster in those situations.

faqs.question: Can my parent get meals on weekends too?
faqs.answer: Most county programs deliver on weekdays only, typically five days a week. Weekend delivery is not standard statewide. Ask your county office what their specific schedule covers. For weekend meals, SNAP benefits or a local food pantry may help fill the gap.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent, or do they have to call themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can initiate the application on their parent's behalf. When you call your county's Area Agency on Aging, tell them you are calling for a parent and provide your parent's name, address, and date of birth. The needs assessment may still involve speaking with your parent directly, either by phone or in person, but you can get the process started and handle most of the paperwork.

faqs.question: My parent's spouse also lives at home. Can the spouse get a meal too?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Some counties will extend a meal to a spouse of an approved participant, but this is not automatic and not guaranteed statewide. Ask about it specifically when you contact your county's Area Agency on Aging. The spouse does not go through a separate full intake, but the county will need to know they are in the household.

programs.name: New Jersey SSI State Supplement
programs.tagline: If your parent is 65 or older with little to no income, they may qualify for up to $1,025 per month in combined federal and state cash support, paid automatically once SSI is approved.

localEntities.name: Social Security Administration offices statewide
NJ Division of Disability Determination Services for SSI claims handling in New Jersey

programs.intro:
If your parent is 65 or older and living on little to no income, New Jersey adds a cash supplement on top of the federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payment. There is no separate New Jersey application. The state supplement is paid automatically once your parent qualifies for SSI through Social Security.

The combined monthly amount depends on where your parent lives. A person living alone in their own home can receive up to $1,025.25 per month in 2026. Someone in a licensed residential health care facility can receive up to $1,204.05 per month. The amount is lower if your parent lives in someone else's household and receives support and maintenance from them, dropping to $706.98 per month in that situation.

To qualify, your parent's gross monthly income must be at or below $1,025.25 (for a single person) and their countable assets must stay under $2,000. The asset limit is strict: modest savings above that threshold can disqualify them. If your parent is already receiving SSI, they are already getting New Jersey's supplement. If they are not yet enrolled, the only door is a federal SSI application through Social Security.
programs.savingsRange: Up to $1,025.25/month for a single person living alone ($12,303/year); up to $1,204.05/month for someone in a licensed residential health care facility ($14,448.60/year) — 2026 combined federal and state amounts.
programs.savingsSource: SSA official 2026 payment amounts for New Jersey SSI recipients, published at ssa.gov/ssi. These are combined federal SSI plus New Jersey state supplement maximums, which vary by living arrangement.

Gross monthly income at or below $1,025.25 (individual) or $1,516.35 (couple) in 2026
Must be a New Jersey resident
No separate NJ application required; approved SSI recipients receive the supplement automatically

countedAssets: Other countable resources as defined by SSA under federal SSI rules
exemptAssets: Some assets are excluded under federal SSI rules; the full list of exemptions is governed by SSA, not a New Jersey-specific rule. Verify exemptions with SSA before applying.

Must live in a qualifying New Jersey living arrangement; the monthly payment amount changes based on whether your parent lives alone, with a spouse, in someone else's home, or in a licensed facility
Must meet all federal SSI nonfinancial requirements as determined by SSA

applicationGuide.summary: Apply directly with Social Security by phone, online at ssa.gov, or in person at a local SSA office; there is no separate New Jersey supplement application.

steps.title: Check income and asset limits before you call
steps.description: Your parent's gross monthly income must be at or below $1,025.25 (single person) and countable assets must be under $2,000. Cash and bank balances count toward that limit. If your parent owns their home and lives in it, that typically does not count as an asset under SSI rules, but verify with SSA.

steps.title: Start the application with Social Security
steps.description: Call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY: 1-800-325-0778), Monday through Friday, 8am to 7pm. You can also begin online at ssa.gov/ssi or visit a local Social Security office. SSA handles the entire SSI process, including New Jersey's supplement.

steps.title: Gather your documents before the interview
steps.description: SSA will schedule a phone or in-person interview to review your parent's information. Bring identification, proof of income, and information about all assets and living arrangements. See the document checklist on this page for the full list.

steps.title: Complete the SSA interview
steps.description: During the interview, SSA will ask about income, assets, living situation, and household members. Be specific about where your parent lives and whether anyone provides them food or housing support, because those answers directly affect the monthly payment amount.

steps.title: Receive the decision and first payment
steps.description: SSA will send a written decision. If approved, the combined federal and New Jersey payment is issued together as one monthly deposit. You do not need to contact a separate New Jersey agency.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Processing time varies. SSA does not publish a standard timeframe for New Jersey SSI applications in the sources available. Applications involving a disability or blindness determination can take longer than age-based applications. Ask SSA when you call.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is 65 or older and is applying based on age alone (not disability), the process is generally faster because SSA does not need to make a separate disability determination. Mention your parent's age upfront when you call.

urls.label: Apply for SSI online at SSA.gov

documentsNeeded: Social Security card (or record of the Social Security number)
Government-issued photo ID such as a driver's license, state ID, or passport
Birth certificate or other proof of age
Most recent Social Security award letter or benefit verification letter (if your parent already receives any Social Security benefit)
Proof of all monthly income: pension statements, retirement account distributions, any wages, or other income sources
Current balances for all checking and savings accounts (SSA will ask for this; bring recent statements or be ready to state the balance)
Information about any other assets: certificates of deposit, stocks, bonds, or other financial accounts
Proof of New Jersey residency, such as a utility bill, lease agreement, or bank statement showing a New Jersey address
Information about the living arrangement: who else lives in the home, whether anyone provides food or financial support, and whether rent is paid
If your parent lives in a licensed residential health care facility, the name and address of the facility
Medicare or Medicaid card if your parent has one (not required, but SSA may ask)
Legal documents if you are applying on behalf of your parent, such as a power of attorney or guardianship papers

contacts.label: Social Security Administration
contacts.description: The only application door for SSI and the New Jersey state supplement. Call to apply, ask eligibility questions, or schedule an in-person appointment at a local SSA office.

contacts.label: SSA TTY Line (for deaf or hard of hearing)
contacts.description: TTY-accessible line for the same SSI application and eligibility questions.

contacts.label: NJ Division of Disability Determination Services
contacts.description: Handles SSI disability determinations for New Jersey applicants under 65 who are applying based on disability or blindness. SSA will route disability cases to this office automatically; you do not contact them separately.

applicationNotes: The New Jersey state supplement is not a separate benefit you apply for. It is added automatically to your parent's SSI check once SSA approves them. If your parent is already getting SSI and living in New Jersey, they are already receiving it.

Where your parent lives changes the monthly payment. A parent living alone gets up to $1,025.25/month. A parent who lives in someone else's household and receives free or reduced-cost food or housing from that person gets only $706.98/month. Be accurate about the living situation when you apply.

The $2,000 asset limit is firm. Even modest savings above that amount can result in denial. Before applying, review bank balances carefully. Some assets, such as the home your parent lives in, are excluded under federal SSI rules, but verify the full list with SSA.

If your parent is 65 or older and does not have a disability, SSA does not need to do a disability determination, which simplifies and can shorten the process. Apply as soon as you believe they may qualify, because SSI does not pay benefits retroactively for months before the application date.

Medicare Savings Programs (Extra Help with Part D premiums)

contentSections.title: Monthly payment by living situation (2026)
contentSections.content: Living alone or with others in own household: $1,025.25/month. Living with a spouse not eligible for SSI: $1,146.99/month. Living in someone else's household receiving support and maintenance: $706.98/month. Living in a licensed residential health care facility: $1,204.05/month. Living in a public general hospital or Medicaid-approved long-term care facility: $50.00/month. Couple living alone or with others: $1,475.35/month. Couple in someone else's household: $1,059.75/month. Couple in a licensed residential health care facility: $2,188.35/month. Source: SSA 2026 payment amounts for New Jersey.

contentSections.title: Why the living arrangement matters so much
contentSections.content: SSI payment amounts are not the same for every recipient. The federal rules reduce the payment when someone provides your parent with free or discounted food or housing, because SSA treats that support as income. If your parent moves in with you and you cover their meals and rent without charging them market rate, their monthly SSI payment can drop to the 'living in someone else's household' rate of $706.98/month rather than the $1,025.25/month rate for someone living independently. This is one of the most common surprises families encounter after a parent moves in. Discuss the living arrangement honestly with SSA during the application.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home. Does that count against the $2,000 asset limit?
faqs.answer: Under federal SSI rules, the home your parent lives in is generally excluded from countable resources and does not count toward the $2,000 limit. However, a second property, a vacation home, or a property they do not live in would typically count. Verify your parent's specific situation with SSA at 1-800-772-1213 before assuming any property is excluded.

faqs.question: My parent already receives Social Security retirement benefits. Can they still qualify?
faqs.answer: Yes, but their Social Security retirement income counts toward the $1,025.25/month gross income limit. SSI excludes the first $20 of any income, so a person receiving $1,005 or less in monthly Social Security income may still be eligible. The SSI payment would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by countable income above excluded amounts, so the actual check may be small. It is still worth applying if income is close to the limit.

faqs.question: My parent moved in with me to save money. Will that change what they receive?
faqs.answer: Probably yes. If your parent lives in your home and you provide food or housing at no charge or below market rate, SSA applies the 'in-kind support and maintenance' rules, which reduce the monthly SSI payment. In 2026, a person in that situation receives $706.98/month instead of $1,025.25/month. If your parent pays their fair share of household expenses, the reduction may not apply. Discuss the details with SSA when you apply.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SSI on behalf of my parent if they cannot manage it themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A family member or other representative can apply on behalf of a parent who is unable to manage their own affairs. You may need to show legal authority such as a power of attorney, or SSA may designate you as a 'representative payee' who receives and manages the benefit on your parent's behalf. Bring any legal documents you have to the application interview.

faqs.question: How long will the application take?
faqs.answer: SSA does not publish a standard processing time for New Jersey SSI applications. Applications for adults 65 or older who qualify based on age (not disability) typically move faster because there is no separate disability determination. Applications involving a disability claim may take several months. Ask SSA directly when you call 1-800-772-1213, as timelines can vary by office workload.

faqs.question: My parent qualifies for both SSI and Medicaid. Should they apply for both separately?
faqs.answer: In New Jersey, SSI recipients are generally automatically enrolled in Medicaid. You do not need to submit a separate Medicaid application for your parent once SSI is approved. Confirm automatic Medicaid enrollment with SSA or the New Jersey Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services after approval, since Medicaid coverage can significantly reduce out-of-pocket medical costs.

faqs.question: What if my parent's income or assets go over the limit after they are approved?
faqs.answer: Your parent is required to report changes in income, assets, or living arrangements to SSA. Exceeding the $2,000 asset limit or the income threshold can reduce or end the benefit. Report changes promptly by calling 1-800-772-1213. Failure to report changes can result in an overpayment that SSA will require your parent to pay back.

faqs.question: Can my parent receive SSI and SNAP at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. SSI and SNAP are separate programs and your parent can receive both. In fact, SSI recipients in New Jersey may be categorically eligible for SNAP, which can simplify that application. Apply for SNAP through the New Jersey Division of Family Development or at nj.gov/humanservices/dfd/programs/.

stateOverview.intro:
New Jersey offers 8 senior programs that could save your loved one hundreds to thousands of dollars annually. These range from property tax relief (up to $6,500 back through Stay NJ) to prescription drug assistance ($5-7 copays instead of full prices) to respite care while you work. Most programs target specific needs, housing costs, medical expenses, or caregiver support, rather than general financial assistance.

Start by checking if your loved one qualifies for property tax relief or prescription assistance, as these typically offer the largest savings. Then look into caregiver support programs if you're providing daily care. Each program has different income limits and requirements, so your loved one may qualify for some but not others.

Several programs are linked, if your loved one qualifies for PAAD, they automatically qualify for Lifeline Credit utility assistance.
stateOverview.resourcesVsBenefits: Most New Jersey senior programs are qualification-based benefits requiring specific income limits, age requirements, or care needs. For example, PAAD requires income under $54,943/year, while JACC requires nursing-level care assessment. Only one program (Senior Freeze) functions as a general resource with broader eligibility. Unlike some states that offer universal information services, New Jersey focuses on targeted financial assistance for those who meet specific criteria.
